name: Rork
tagline: Prompt-driven builder that generates cross-platform mobile apps as React Native / Expo projects and previews them on your phone.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Credit-metered plans are the norm in this category, so real cost tracks how much you generate, not the sticker.

verdictSummary: Rork is an AI coding agent with a mobile-shaped harness bolted on, which makes it an awkward thing to defend against AI coding agents. What you actually pay for is the wrapper: a project template, a live preview on a real phone, and an edit-run-fix loop you never have to configure. All three of those are commodity Expo tooling, and a competent agent can wire them into a local folder in an afternoon. Once you have an Expo Router project plus tunneled dev server plus your agent of choice reading the file tree, the prompt-to-app loop is intact and the token spend is yours instead of resold as credits. The part that does not survive DIY is the frictionless path from prompt to something in the App Store, which is Apple's fault, not Rork's.
coreLoopDIY: Scaffolds an opinionated Expo Router project with a tunneled dev server and QR preview, plus agent instructions so you can describe screens in plain English and watch them hot-reload on your phone.
requirements: Expo Go installed on a physical phone, or a simulator if you already have Xcode / Android Studio
A coding agent you already pay for, which is doing the actual generation
An Expo account only if you later want EAS cloud builds
whatYouLose: Hosted builds and the assisted path to TestFlight and the Play Store, which is the genuinely annoying part of shipping mobile
A preview that works for someone with zero local toolchain, including non-technical collaborators
Bundled backend, auth and storage defaults, so you pick and wire your own
Automatic error capture and self-repair loops when the bundler or a native module explodes
Shareable app links you can text to someone without explaining what a tunnel is
moatNotes: The moat is the last mile: build infrastructure, signing, store submission and a preview that works for people who have never opened a terminal. The code generation part is not the moat, it is the commodity.
whyPeopleStillPay: Two groups keep paying. Non-developers, for whom local Expo tooling is not a weekend project but a wall, and the hosted preview plus build pipeline is the entire product. And developers who can absolutely do this themselves but do not want to spend a Saturday on provisioning profiles, EAS config and simulator drift when they just wanted to test an idea on their own phone. Neither of those is irrational. Both stop being true the moment you already run a coding agent locally and have shipped one mobile app before, at which point you are renting a template.
notes: Wrappers around coding agents are structurally hard to defend from coding agents; the interesting question is whether you need a store build or just a thing on your own phone.
prompt:
Build a local prompt-to-mobile-app workspace in this empty folder. Stack is fixed: Expo (latest SDK) with expo-router, TypeScript strict, React Native, zustand for state, AsyncStorage for persistence. No web dashboard, no accounts, no telemetry, no multi-tenant anything.

Do this:
1. Scaffold an Expo Router project with TypeScript in the current folder. Use a tabs layout: app/_layout.tsx, app/(tabs)/index.tsx, app/(tabs)/settings.tsx.
2. Create components/ui/ with a small opinionated kit: Screen, Card, Button, TextField, ListRow, EmptyState. Plain StyleSheet, no styling framework. One theme file with colors, spacing, radii, type scale, and light/dark support via useColorScheme.
3. Create lib/store.ts: a zustand store persisted to AsyncStorage with a hydrate-on-boot guard, plus a demo slice (a list of items with add, toggle, delete) so the template runs with real state on first launch.
4. Add lib/api.ts: a typed fetch wrapper reading EXPO_PUBLIC_API_BASE from .env. Ship .env.example only, never commit .env, and add .env to .gitignore.
5. Add scripts to package.json: "dev" runs expo start --tunnel and prints the QR code, "dev:lan" runs expo start, "typecheck" runs tsc --noEmit, "lint" runs eslint. Wire eslint and prettier with sane defaults.
6. Write AGENTS.md at the root: where screens live, how to add a route, how to add a store slice, which components to reuse, the rule that new screens must be typed and dark-mode safe, and an instruction to run typecheck after every change.
7. Write README.md with exact first-run steps: install deps, install Expo Go on the phone, run dev, scan the QR, then describe the screen you want to a coding agent and let it edit files while the app hot-reloads.
8. Add a docs/RECIPES.md with three short worked examples: add a detail screen with route params, add a form that writes to the store, add a list backed by a remote fetch with loading and error states.

Out of scope, do not build: EAS or store submission config, native modules requiring a custom dev client, push notifications, auth providers, any backend, any hosted preview service.

When done, run typecheck and confirm the dev server starts. Report the exact command sequence for a cold start and stop.
